claims.text: The Alter Hof (Old Court) was built in the late 12th century and served as the first permanent imperial residence in the Holy Roman Empire under Emperor Louis IV.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: The building complex consists of five wings named Burgstock, Zwingerstock, Lorenzistock, Pfisterstock, and Brunnenstock.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: The former St. Lorenz Chapel, which stood on the north side until its demolition in the 19th century, once housed the crown jewels and regalia of the House of Wittelsbach.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: Following citizen uprisings that made the old castle feel unsafe, the ruling dukes eventually built a new fortress further out that would become the modern Munich Residenz.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: By the 16th century, the royal residence was permanently moved to the new fortress, and the Alter Hof was relegated to housing various governmental departments.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: A modern equestrian statue of Emperor Louis IV, created by sculptor Hans Wimmer, stands on the northern exterior of the complex.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: In 1914, a young Adolf Hitler painted a watercolor depicting the building, known as 'The Courtyard of the Old Residency in Munich'.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: The complex was heavily destroyed during World War II and underwent significant reconstruction in the post-war period.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: In 2001, a highly controversial redevelopment project saw the Brunnenstock and Pfisterstock wings completely demolished and replaced with modern structures by private investors.
claims.subject: self
